title: Are these not men? (1511)
hookLine: Antonio de Montesinos preaches on Hispaniola against the colonists' cruelty to Indigenous people

lines: THE COLONY'S LEADING MEN IN THE PEWS.
A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.
cards: Advent, on the island of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean. A rough church, and in it the leading men of the Spanish colony, who hold Indigenous people as forced laborers in the mines and fields.

A Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbs up to preach. His text is from John's Gospel, John the Baptist describing himself. In the Douay-Rheims: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness."
Then he tells them who the wilderness is. It's them. Today, the sermon, and the question at the heart of it.

teach.b: You met this sermon briefly on day eight hundred thirty-nine; today, its words. It survives because Bartolomé de las Casas wrote it down in his history of the Indies.

As he tells it, Montesinos said everyone listening was living in mortal sin because of the cruelty and tyranny they used against these innocent people. Then came the questions, which Las Casas records in substance.
By what right do you hold these people in such cruel servitude? Why do you work them until they fall sick and die? Then today's line: are these not men?
Do they not have rational souls? Are you not bound to love them as you love yourselves? That last question is Jesus's own command, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

Montesinos didn't speak alone. Las Casas says the friars of his house agreed on the sermon together and put their names to it. The furious colonists went to the friars' house and demanded he take it back the next Sunday.

teach.h: TAKE IT BACK. HE PREACHED IT AGAIN.
teach.b: He came back, climbed up again, and preached the same truth, harder. It didn't end the cruelty. The sermon set off arguments that reached the Spanish court.
And one man in that colony, Las Casas himself, who held laborers too, later gave them up, became a Dominican, and spent his life defending Indigenous people.

teach.h: LOVE THEM AS YOU LOVE YOURSELVES.
teach.b: Friars of the Church named the sin of the Church's own people, out loud, to their faces. Veritas, told when it cost something.

how: Dominicans remember Antonio de Montesinos's Advent sermon as part of their tradition of preaching for human dignity, and Catholic teaching on the dignity of every person is often taught alongside the story of Montesinos and Bartolomé de las Casas.

games.q: what does “are these not men?” mean?
o: a line from the Psalms about human weakness
a pope's question about which men may become priests
a friar's challenge to colonists abusing Indigenous people

games.q: the sermon on Hispaniola — tap the pairs.
p: wrote it down, later became a Dominican
a voice crying in the wilderness

s: Montesinos preached on his own, against his community's wishes

games.q: you're Montesinos. the colony's leading men come to your house, furious, and demand you take back your sermon next Sunday. what do you do?
o: take it back, to keep the peace.
soften it, and talk about something gentler.
climb up next Sunday and preach it again.
games.why: he preached it again, harder. the sermon didn't end the cruelty, but it started arguments that reached the Spanish court. Las Casas, who wrote it down, later became a Dominican himself.

practice: Bring to mind someone in your world who is easy to look past, the person who cleans the office at night, someone talked about as a problem and never as a person, and hold their face, or picture one.
Let Montesinos's question sit beside it, are these not people, with a soul and a story; if you pray, pray for them by name if you know it, and if not, simply keep their face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Are these not men? A Dominican's question to colonists who were working Indigenous people to death. This week ran from veritas to the truth told when it cost something. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, John 1:23 in the Vulgate: I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, the text of the sermon.

carryVoice: Your line: are these not men. Asked to the powerful, and asked again the next Sunday. See you tomorrow.
